About me

I started in software engineering and found my home in the space between people and screens. I like knowing why someone got stuck, so I run the research, design the fix, test it again, and measure the difference.

That’s why this portfolio has two sides: design work you can click through, and dashboards I built myself to analyze usability results.

OrganizedEvery project starts with a plan, a process and clear documentation.
ExplorerI ask users, test ideas early and follow the findings.

Tajah: a talent platform for Saudi women in sport

My graduation project, built over two semesters by a team of six. Tajah connects female athletes with sports clubs through one structured, fair and accessible platform, so talent gets discovered by performance instead of personal connections. Arabic, right-to-left, and live at tajahsa.com.

43.75%of talent discovery relies on personal networks and WhatsApp

21 → 0WCAG 2.1 AA issues found in the audit, all resolved through iteration

Testing changed the design

After the first version, usability testing with 8 participants (4 athletes, 4 club representatives) showed what to fix. These are the changes that came out of it:

FoundFixed

Finding the main tabs

Main tabs were hard to notice and took extra steps. The team added quick shortcuts on the home page.

FoundFixed

Color contrast

The WCAG audit found failures from too much yellow. Yellow was cut back and no participant reported readability problems afterward.

FoundFixed

Accidental submissions

In GP1, tapping Apply sent the request straight away without asking “Are you sure?”, so users could apply by mistake. The team added a confirmation dialog, and nobody submitted by accident in the second round.

Data analyst corner

I analyzed the Tajah usability tests myself. I first cleaned and organized the data in Power Query, then built six Power BI dashboards from the results: an overview, a detailed analysis and a survey analysis for each of the two user groups. They cover completion rate, errors, time on task, clicks and feedback themes.

90%completion rate, clubs (4 participants, 28 errors)
97.5%completion rate, players (4 participants, 25 errors)
30.75 vs 14.5average clicks per session: clubs vs players

Each group had 4 participants, so these figures are exploratory. They show where friction appeared and are not statistically representative.

Dashboards from my coursework

More projects

ChicCloset

A secondhand luxury fashion marketplace concept for Saudi Arabia, built by a team of five for an HCI prototyping course. A competitive analysis and a 150-respondent survey showed that seller credibility (34%) and product quality (32.7%) were buyers’ biggest worries, so the app is built around trust: an authenticity guarantee, seller reviews and ratings, and direct contact with sellers.

My part: sketching and designing the advanced search (by category, search icon or menu), the direct buyer–seller inquiry flow and the seller profit-margin transparency feature, starting from my own hand-drawn ideation sketch. Moderated tests with 6 participants, using Think-Aloud, reached a 100% task completion rate for buyers and sellers, and the top recommendations were Arabic localization and product filtering.

MyFood

An accessible recipe-sharing website built by a team of five for an Inclusive Design course. The team used the W5H approach, an empathy map and wireframes, then built the pages and added WAI-ARIA attributes, checking them with the NVDA screen reader.

My part: I built the Recipe Details page (the team collaborated on the remaining 10%). I added aria-controls and aria-expanded to the Recipes dropdown, so screen readers know the link controls the menu and whether it is open, and verified it with NVDA.

I also audited Absher’s website with WAVE, Accessibility Cloud Lite and Silktide, plus manual tests with keyboard, NVDA, zoom and animation. Accessibility Cloud Lite found 31 issues (17 critical). Manual testing found no skip-to-content link, an unusable layout at 400% zoom, and animated banners with no pause control. I wrote up suggested fixes for each.

Mundialist

Team project

A World Cup 2034 tourist guide app for Saudi Arabia: match tickets, trip plans, maps and cultural guides in one place, for visitors who come for the football and stay to explore. Built by a team of five for a UI Design course.

We ran a survey and interviews, wrote three personas (a footballer, a YouTuber and a mother planning her son’s birthday trip) and mapped the information structure before drawing wireframes. Users asked most for quick access to emergency services, easier maps, and help with tickets and visas. The visual design uses a lavender-and-green palette inspired by Saudi landscapes, Roboto and a custom icon set, and the screens were built as a clickable prototype in Uizard.

We tested the prototype with one participant and ran focus-prediction heatmaps on every screen. The interface was clear and easy to understand, but the path to hotel booking was hard to find, so that is where we would improve first.

HAJJ & UMRAH UX Project

Team project

Arafat Boundary Verification System: a safety-critical concept for the Day of Arafat. A smart wristband tells pilgrims, through vibration patterns alone, whether they are inside the Arafat boundary. Between 12:00 and 18:00 the plain is 42–48°C with 2–3 million people, unreliable signal and no landmarks, so screens and text cannot be relied on. Built by a team of five for an HCI course.

Instead of a standard persona, we modeled the pilgrim’s temporary state under heat, fatigue and anxiety, and left out positivity-biased social media posts from our sources. The system has a five-state model (Normal, Advisory, Warning, Danger, Emergency), each with its own vibration pattern, an offline GPS boundary check with a 50 m buffer, and a group-leader app. We designed 13 screens (6 mobile, 7 wristband) and evaluated them with Nielsen’s heuristics and a cognitive walkthrough.

The concept was my idea, and the screens were designed with Figma Make.

ChicCloset screens

ChicCloset: my part, explained

The prototyping course report linked every design decision to a behavioral or persuasion principle. The ideas started from the whole team: each member sketched solutions on their own, then we met and chose the best ones. My sketch covered advanced search, direct buyer–seller inquiries and price transparency for sellers. The screens below show where those ideas ended up in the team’s prototype. Other examples from the team’s report: a reservation countdown (loss aversion), a first-order discount and a seller photo guide (reciprocity), and seller reviews (social validation).

ChicCloset design system

A Figma component library built by the team of five for the Design Systems course. The prototype started in Uizard and was rebuilt in Figma. After feedback on readability and accessibility, the palette was revised and the three typefaces were cut down to one, Red Hat Display. Team project
